promptText: What specific problem does MCP solve that plain function/tool calling (as introduced in earlier tool-calling chapters) does not?
options: MCP makes the underlying model reason more accurately about when to call a tool

MCP standardizes discovery and invocation so a tool built once as an independent server can be reused across many applications, reducing an N-applications-by-M-systems integration problem to roughly N+M
MCP replaces JSON entirely with a faster binary wire format
MCP eliminates the need for any authentication between a client and a server
explanation: Tool calling defines how a model requests an action, but says nothing about where the implementation lives or how it's shared across applications; MCP standardizes that transport/discovery layer, turning N×M bespoke integrations into N+M.

promptText: MCP defines three participant roles. Which set correctly names them?
options: Publisher, Subscriber, Broker
Host, Client, Server
Manager, Worker, Reducer
Sender, Receiver, Relay
explanation: The Host is the AI application itself, the Client is a component inside the host maintaining a 1:1 session with one server, and the Server is an independent process exposing capabilities over the protocol.

promptText: MCP servers expose three capability primitives — tools, resources, and prompts. Who typically decides when each one is used?
options: Tools: the model autonomously; Resources: the host/user attaching context deliberately; Prompts: the user selecting a template explicitly
All three are always decided exclusively by the model during inference
All three are always decided exclusively by the server, never the client or model
Tools: the user; Resources: the model; Prompts: the server, with no human involvement
explanation: Tools are invoked at the model's discretion mid-reasoning, resources are attached as deliberate background context, and prompts are reusable templates the user selects explicitly, bypassing the model's own judgment.

promptText: Why did MCP build on top of JSON-RPC 2.0 instead of inventing a new wire format?
options: JSON-RPC is the only format that supports streaming

It reuses an already-standardized, transport-agnostic message format with mature parsers in every language, letting MCP focus its novelty on the vocabulary of tools/resources/prompts rather than reinventing a wire protocol
JSON-RPC was created specifically for MCP by the same team
JSON-RPC eliminates the need for an initialize handshake
explanation: Good infrastructure standards reuse boring, well-understood primitives underneath and add value only in the genuinely novel layer — here, the vocabulary of tools, resources, and prompts.

promptText: The stdio transport spawns an MCP server as a local subprocess and communicates over stdin/stdout. What deployment scenario is it a poor fit for?
options: A single-user desktop IDE integration
Local development and testing
A multi-tenant, server-side production deployment, since it would require spawning and supervising one OS process per concurrent user session
Any scenario at all — stdio is always the correct production transport
explanation: Spawning a process per request doesn't scale and reintroduces the per-request resource overhead that connection pooling exists to eliminate; production server-side hosts should use remote, pooled connections over Streamable HTTP instead.

promptText: MCP's "sampling" capability surprises many engineers on first read. What does it let a server do?
options: Randomly sample which tool to call next instead of letting the model decide
Ask the host's LLM to generate a completion on the server's behalf, flowing in the opposite direction from a normal tool call
Cache tool results to reduce latency on repeated calls
Sample multiple hosts simultaneously to pick the fastest one
explanation: Sampling lets server-side logic compose LLM calls into its own capability logic (e.g., summarizing a diff) using the host's model access, without the server needing its own model integration — a well-implemented host requires explicit approval before honoring it.

promptText: What is the "confused deputy" risk in an MCP deployment, and how is it best mitigated?
options: It occurs when a server crashes mid-session; mitigated by automatic subprocess restart

A host authenticates with one broad service-level credential and triggers calls on behalf of many end users; if the server doesn't separately verify the requesting end user's authorization, the host's broad credential can bypass per-user authorization — mitigated by propagating end-user identity and enforcing authorization per call at the server
It occurs when two servers expose a tool with the same name; mitigated by host-side namespacing
It is a JSON-RPC parsing ambiguity; mitigated by upgrading the protocol version
explanation: This is the classical access-control 'confused deputy' problem applied to the tool-invocation layer: never assume host-level authentication implies per-user authorization.

promptText: What is the "tool poisoning" or "rug-pull" attack pattern specific to MCP, and why is a one-time server review insufficient defense?
options: A server's tool descriptions are fetched live via tools/list and can change later via list_changed, so a server reviewed and approved as benign can silently swap in manipulated tool descriptions afterward, which a single point-in-time review cannot catch
It refers to a server deliberately returning HTTP 500 errors to exhaust client retry budgets
It is when a client sends malformed JSON-RPC that crashes the server process
It only affects servers using the stdio transport, never remote HTTP servers
explanation: Because tool metadata is fetched dynamically rather than fixed at approval time, defending against tool poisoning requires pinning and diffing approved tool definitions across versions rather than trusting a one-time review to hold indefinitely.

promptText: Why does the idempotentHint tool annotation matter specifically for how a host implements retries after a network timeout?
options: It has no practical effect on retry logic, it is purely documentation

After a timeout the host cannot know whether the call executed before the timeout or never arrived; blindly retrying is only safe if the operation is idempotent, so idempotentHint tells the host whether auto-retry is safe or whether it must surface an ambiguous-failure state instead
It tells the host how many times a tool may be called per session
It is required for a tool to appear in tools/list at all
explanation: Re-running a non-idempotent call like create_ticket after an ambiguous timeout risks creating duplicates — idempotentHint lets the host distinguish tools it can safely auto-retry from ones needing explicit confirmation.

promptText: What is one of the single most common real-world bugs when authoring a stdio-based MCP server?
options: Forgetting to implement the tools/call method
Writing debug/log output to stdout, which corrupts the JSON-RPC message stream since stdout is the exclusive channel carrying protocol messages back to the client in the stdio transport
Using an unsupported programming language
Setting protocolVersion incorrectly in every single request
explanation: A single stray print statement to stdout desynchronizes or breaks the client's JSON-RPC parsing; log output must go to stderr or MCP's own logging notification instead.

promptText: If a host connects to two MCP servers that each expose a tool literally named search, how does the protocol expect this collision to be handled?
options: MCP automatically deduplicates identical tool names across servers
The protocol itself does not resolve this — it is the host's responsibility to namespace or qualify each tool name (e.g., docs_search vs crm_search) and maintain a mapping back to the correct server
The second server to register the name is silently disabled
The client refuses to connect to the second server entirely
explanation: MCP does not solve naming collisions across independently-developed servers for you — the host must disambiguate before presenting a merged tool list to the model.

promptText: How does Streamable HTTP improve on the earlier, more rigid SSE-based remote transport MCP originally used?
options: It requires a permanently open, long-lived connection before any communication can begin

It folds plain request/response and streaming into a single POST/response endpoint, letting the server upgrade to a Server-Sent Events stream only when needed, without pre-agreeing on streaming up front
It eliminates JSON-RPC entirely in favor of raw binary frames
It removes the need for an initialize handshake
explanation: The earlier transport required opening a long-lived SSE connection up front for all server-to-client messages; Streamable HTTP negotiates within a single POST/response pair, which is friendlier to ordinary load balancers and proxies.

promptText: Why is "the model never talks to the MCP server directly" considered a security-relevant architectural property, not merely a design detail?
options: Because it means the model can never be tricked by injected content at all

Because every tool-call request the model produces still passes through the host's orchestration layer, giving the host a mandatory interception point to apply authorization checks, confirmation prompts, and rate limiting on every call, regardless of how many servers are connected
Because it guarantees the server cannot ever return malformed data
Because it removes the need for any authentication between host and server
explanation: If the model could reach servers directly, none of the host-mediated policy enforcement (authorization, confirmation, logging) would have anywhere to attach — the host-mediated call is precisely what makes centralized security controls possible.

promptText: You are designing a host-side gateway aggregating 50 internal MCP servers for every AI application in a company. Which combination of design decisions is most essential?
options: Give every consuming application its own copy of each server's credentials so the gateway itself never needs to store any secrets

Namespace tool names across servers, maintain a cached aggregated capability catalog refreshed on list_changed, centralize per-server credential/auth-scope management in the gateway, and apply per-server circuit breaking so one slow server doesn't stall the other 49
Force every one of the 50 servers to migrate to the exact same programming language for consistency
Disable tools/list caching entirely so every request always gets a perfectly fresh view of all 50 servers
explanation: These are the core decisions the chapter names for a 50-server gateway: disambiguation, a central discovered/cached catalog, centralized credential management, and per-server failure isolation — the gateway itself then becomes a shared dependency that needs the same production rigor as the servers it fronts.

promptText: Why does connecting a dozen MCP servers to a host "just in case" have a real, easily-overlooked cost even if the model never ends up calling most of their tools?
options: Because MCP charges a flat per-connection licensing fee

Because every connected server's tool (and often resource/prompt) schemas are typically folded into the tool-schema payload sent with every single model call, inflating prompt tokens and therefore cost and latency on every turn regardless of whether those tools are ever invoked
Because MCP servers must be re-authenticated on every single message exchanged
Because connecting more than three servers is technically disallowed by the specification
explanation: Twelve servers averaging ten tools each is 120 tool schemas riding along on every conversational turn — measuring token cost attributable specifically to tool schemas per server is how you identify which connected servers are dead weight.
